analysis.one_liner: Caps consumer class-action damages against credit reporting firms at $500,000 and bans punitive damages.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a vote after being referred to two House committees in May 2017, leaving the Fair Credit Reporting Act's class-action liability rules unchanged.
analysis.plain_summary: The Fair Credit Reporting Act lets consumers sue credit bureaus and other companies that misuse their credit data. In a class action, a company that willfully violates the law can owe each consumer $100 to $1,000 — even without proof of actual financial harm — plus punitive damages. This bill would have capped a class's total recovery at the lesser of $500,000 or 1% of the company's net worth, eliminated the per-person minimum, and banned punitive damages entirely [S2][S3]. For a large credit bureau, the cap would often amount to 1% of net worth — a small fraction of what a nationwide data-misuse class action can produce. The bill never advanced past committee referrals [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Credit reporting agencies and any company that furnishes or handles consumer credit data. Under current law, a willful violation carries statutory damages of $100-$1,000 per class member, so a class of millions can produce nine- or ten-figure exposure. The bill would cap that at the lesser of $500,000 or 1% of net worth and eliminate punitive damages, sharply reducing the financial risk of mishandling consumer credit data [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Caps total class recovery against a willful FCRA violator at the lesser of $500,000 or 1% of the defendant's net worth, replacing unlimited per-person statutory damages of $100-$1,000 per member [S2][S3].
Eliminates punitive damages for willful FCRA violations by striking the punitive-damages provision from the statute [S2][S3].
Removes the statutory minimum damages floor for class members, so a court could award nothing to individual consumers even when a violation is proven [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers harmed by credit-reporting errors, identity theft, or misuse of their credit data. Their practical remedy in a class action would shrink dramatically: no guaranteed minimum per person, a hard ceiling on the whole class's recovery, and no punitive damages — which reduces both compensation and the financial pressure on companies to keep consumer data accurate and secure [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill allows class members to receive no individual recovery at all, since the court may not apply any minimum per-member damages, and the entire class recovery could be as low as $500,000 no matter how many consumers were harmed [S3].

Supporters argued that FCRA's statutory damages — available without proof of actual harm — can produce class recoveries wildly out of proportion to consumers' real losses and invite litigation aimed at settlements rather than correction; the cap and punitive-damages ban were pitched as keeping FCRA class actions proportionate. An honest supporter would concede the trade-off: the same exposure that looks disproportionate also is what makes companies fix their data practices, and 1% of net worth can be a rounding error for a large credit bureau.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit accrues almost entirely to a narrow set of large companies that would see their worst-case class-action liability fall from potentially hundreds of millions of dollars to a fixed cap, while the cost falls on consumers whose main realistic enforcement tool against credit-data misuse — the class action — would be largely defanged. There is a genuine argument that FCRA's per-violation statutory damages can over-punish technical violations, but this bill addressed that by removing the remedy's teeth entirely rather than tailoring it, and it was never debated or amended in committee.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Financial Services and Judiciary committees, one subcommittee took a hearing, and neither committee ever voted to send it to the House floor, so it died when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Loudermilk introduced the bill on May 4, 2017, with Reps. Royce, Budd, King of New York, and Wagner as original cosponsors [S3].

It was referred to both the Financial Services Committee and the Judiciary Committee; the Judiciary Committee later referred it to its Subcommittee on the Constitution and Civil Justice on June 7, 2017 [S5].
The only substantive action in its two-year life was a subcommittee hearing on financial institutions and consumer credit on September 7, 2017; no committee ever marked up or reported the bill [S5].
The bill attracted 13 cosponsors, all Republicans, and never received a floor vote in either chamber [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers who rely on the FCRA's class-action remedy came out ahead, because the current law's full damages — statutory damages per member and punitive damages — remain on the books. Credit bureaus and data-handling firms remain exposed to the liability the bill sought to cap.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 supporters — the sponsor and 13 cosponsors — were Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored, and the bill died without a vote in the Republican-controlled House.

industries.note: The bill would cap their worst-case FCRA class-action liability at the lesser of $500,000 or 1% of net worth and eliminate punitive damages — the exact companies most exposed to large FCRA class actions over reporting errors and data breaches. For a large bureau, 1% of net worth is a modest sum, so the cap would shield them from most of the financial consequence of mishandling consumer data.

industries.industry: Banks, lenders, and companies that furnish consumer credit data
industries.note: Anyone who reports or uses consumer credit information can be sued under the FCRA; the bill's cap would have applied to them too, lowering their exposure when they furnish inaccurate data.

A hard cap on class recovery plus a ban on punitive damages would shrink the fee base for consumer class actions, making many FCRA cases uneconomical to bring. Consumers lose the enforcement these suits provide.
